original_question: Which gene, associated with the two most common mutations causing nemaline myopathy, encodes a protein whose length is proportional to the length of the thin filament?

final_qi.question: Which gene, associated with the two most common mutations causing nemaline myopathy, encodes a protein whose length is proportional to the length of the thin filament?
final_qi.long_answer: The NEB gene is one of the two loci most frequently mutated in nemaline myopathy (the other being ACTA1). NEB encodes nebulin, a giant actin-binding protein that functions as a molecular ruler: the size of each nebulin molecule scales with, and thereby specifies, the length of the skeletal-muscle thin filament. Thus, NEB is the gene whose product’s length is directly proportional to thin-filament length.

final_answer.long_answer: The gene NEB encodes the giant skeletal-muscle protein nebulin. NEB and ACTA1 account for the two most frequent mutation sources in nemaline myopathy. Nebulin’s molecular length scales with—and helps specify—the length of the actin thin filament in sarcomeres, making NEB the gene whose protein length is proportional to thin-filament length.

final_answer.long_answer: The NEB gene, one of the two most frequently mutated genes in nemaline myopathy (the other being ACTA1), encodes the giant sarcomeric protein nebulin. Nebulin spans the length of the actin-based thin filament in skeletal muscle, acting as a molecular ruler: the size of the nebulin molecule is directly proportional to, and helps determine, the final length of the thin filament. Loss-of-function or truncating NEB mutations therefore disrupt filament length regulation and are a leading cause of nemaline myopathy.
